questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 43 · Kinds of share capital
questions.stem: Under section 43 of the Companies Act 2013, 'preference share capital' means that part of the issued share capital of a company limited by shares which carries a preferential right with respect to:

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of share capital — ss. 43 to 46 →

options.text: Payment of dividend only
options.explanation: One preferential right is not enough. The Explanation to s. 43 requires BOTH the dividend preference and the capital-repayment preference for the capital to be preference share capital.

options.text: Repayment of capital in the case of winding up only
options.explanation: Again only one limb. A share preferred as to capital but ranking equally as to dividend is not preference share capital.

options.text: Both payment of dividend (a fixed amount or at a fixed rate) and repayment of the amount of the share capital in the case of a winding up
options.explanation: Correct. Section 43(b) read with its Explanation requires both preferential rights; capital which is not preference share capital is, residually, equity share capital.

options.text: Voting on every resolution placed before the company
options.explanation: Voting on every resolution is the equity shareholder's right under s. 47(1); a preference shareholder's voting is restricted by s. 47(2).

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 43 · Differential voting rights
questions.stem: Pravaha Motors Limited proposes to issue equity shares with differential rights as to voting. Which of the following correctly states a condition for the issue under the rules-level framework?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 43(a)(ii); Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules 2014 (amendment-sensitive)

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of share capital — ss. 43 to 46 →

options.text: The articles of association must authorise the issue, and the issue must be approved by an ordinary resolution passed at a general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. The rules require authorisation in the articles and an ordinary resolution (through postal ballot where a listed company is required to use it). The voting-power ceiling and the no-default conditions are further rules-level requirements, all amendment-sensitive.

options.text: A special resolution and the prior approval of the Central Government are required
options.explanation: Neither is required. The rules ask for an ordinary resolution; no Central Government approval enters the DVR framework.

options.text: Only a listed company may issue shares with differential voting rights
options.explanation: Unlisted companies may also issue DVR shares under the rules; listing only changes the mode of approval (postal ballot where applicable).

options.text: Shares with differential rights must be issued as preference shares
options.explanation: Differential rights attach to EQUITY share capital under s. 43(a)(ii); preference capital is a separate kind defined by s. 43(b).

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 45 · Numbering of shares
questions.stem: Regarding the distinctive numbering of shares under section 45 of the Companies Act 2013, which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of share capital — ss. 43 to 46 →

options.text: Every share, including a share held in dematerialised form, must be distinguished by its distinctive number
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 45 carves out exactly this case: numbering does not apply where the holder's name is entered as holder of beneficial interest in the records of a depository.

options.text: Only preference shares need be distinctively numbered
options.explanation: Section 45 draws no distinction between equity and preference shares; the only carve-out is for depository holdings.

options.text: Distinctive numbering is optional in all cases if the articles so provide
options.explanation: The section is mandatory for shares held in physical form; the articles cannot dispense with it.

options.text: Distinctive numbering does not apply to shares held by a person whose name is entered as holder of beneficial interest in such shares in the records of a depository
options.explanation: Correct. Dematerialised shares are fungible, so the proviso to s. 45 disapplies the numbering requirement for them.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 46 · Certificate of shares
questions.stem: A certificate of shares issued under the common seal, if any, of the company or signed in the prescribed manner, specifying the shares held by a person, is:

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of share capital — ss. 43 to 46 →

options.text: Conclusive evidence of the title of the person to the shares
options.explanation: The section says PRIMA FACIE, not conclusive. The company may still show the certificate was issued without authority, and a forged certificate confers no title at all.

options.text: Prima facie evidence of the title of the person to the shares specified in it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 46(1) makes the certificate prima facie evidence of title — a rebuttable starting point, not an unanswerable one.

options.text: Itself the share, so that delivery of the certificate transfers the share
options.explanation: The share is movable property transferable in the manner provided by the articles (s. 44) through the s. 56 machinery; the certificate merely evidences title.

options.text: Evidence of title only if countersigned by the Registrar of Companies
options.explanation: No countersignature by the Registrar is required or provided for; execution is by the company in the prescribed manner.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 47(2) · Preference shareholders' voting
questions.stem: The dividend on the 10% cumulative preference shares of Girisha Papers Limited has remained unpaid for the last three years. At the forthcoming general meeting, the preference shareholders are entitled to vote on:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 47(2) and its second proviso

readLink.label: Read: Voting rights and variation of class rights →

options.text: Every resolution placed before the company
options.explanation: Correct. Where the dividend in respect of a class of preference shares has not been paid for two years or more, that class votes on ALL resolutions — three years of arrears crosses the threshold.

options.text: Only resolutions which directly affect the rights attached to the preference shares
options.explanation: That is the default rule, but it is displaced once the dividend has remained unpaid for two years or more — the arrears here are three years.

options.text: No resolution, since preference shareholders never vote at general meetings
options.explanation: Preference shareholders always vote on resolutions directly affecting their rights, on winding up and on repayment or reduction of capital — and on everything once dividend is two years in arrears.

options.text: Only a resolution for the winding up of the company
options.explanation: Winding up is one of the deemed directly-affecting matters, but the two-year arrears widen the right to every resolution.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 48(2) · Dissent threshold
questions.stem: A class of Vasundhara Textiles Limited consists of 8,00,000 issued preference shares. A variation of the rights attached to the class has been approved by special resolution at a separate class meeting. The MINIMUM number of shares that holders who did not consent to or vote in favour of the variation must hold between them, in order to apply to the Tribunal under section 48(2) for cancellation of the variation, is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 48(2) — holders of not less than 10% of the issued shares of the class

readLink.label: Read: Voting rights and variation of class rights →

options.text: 40,000 shares
options.explanation: That is 5% of the class. Section 48(2) sets the threshold at not less than 10% of the issued shares of the class.

options.text: 80,000 shares
options.explanation: Correct. 10% of 8,00,000 issued shares of the class is 80,000 shares, and the applicants must be holders who did not consent to or vote for the variation. The application must be made within 21 days.

options.text: 1,20,000 shares
options.explanation: That is 15%. The statutory threshold is 10% of the issued shares of the class.

options.text: 2,00,000 shares
options.explanation: That is 25%. The consent threshold under s. 48(1) is three-fourths, but the DISSENT threshold for applying to the Tribunal is only 10%.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 48(1) · Variation affecting another class
questions.stem: A proposed variation of the rights attached to the equity shares of Yamnotri Traders Limited would also affect the rights attached to its preference shares. Under section 48(1), the variation requires:

readLink.label: Read: Voting rights and variation of class rights →

options.text: The consent of three-fourths of the equity class alone, since only equity rights are being varied
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 48(1) is triggered because the variation by one class AFFECTS the rights of another class; the affected class must also consent.

options.text: The prior approval of the Tribunal in every case
options.explanation: The Tribunal enters only on a dissenters' application under s. 48(2); no prior Tribunal approval is required for a consented variation.

options.text: A simple majority of both classes voting together at one general meeting
options.explanation: Class rights are varied class by class — written consent of three-fourths of the issued shares of the class or a special resolution at a SEPARATE class meeting, never a combined simple majority.

options.text: The consent of three-fourths of the equity class and, in addition, the consent of three-fourths of the preference class whose rights are affected
options.explanation: Correct. Where the variation by one class of shareholders affects the rights of any other class, the consent of three-fourths of that other class is also required.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 49–50 · Calls and calls in advance
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about calls on shares and acceptance of unpaid share money in advance is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Calls, advances and proportionate dividend →

options.text: The Board may make calls selectively on some shareholders of a class if it records reasons
options.explanation: Section 49 mandates calls on a uniform basis on all shares falling under the same class; no reasoned selectivity is permitted.

options.text: A member who pays call money in advance under section 50 may vote in respect of the amount so paid from the date of payment
options.explanation: Section 50(2) bars voting rights in respect of the advance until that amount would, but for the advance, become presently payable.

options.text: Calls must be made on a uniform basis on all shares falling under the same class, and shares of the same nominal value on which different amounts have been paid up are not deemed to fall under the same class
options.explanation: Correct. That is s. 49 with its Explanation — the different paid-up amounts place the shares in different classes for the purpose of the uniformity rule.

options.text: A company may accept calls in advance only with the sanction of the Tribunal
options.explanation: No Tribunal sanction is involved; s. 50(1) needs only authorisation by the articles.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 51 · Dividend in proportion to paid-up amount
questions.stem: The articles of Nandini Agrotech Limited authorise payment of dividend in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share, as permitted by section 51. The company declares a dividend of 12%. Tanvi holds 5,000 equity shares of ₹10 each on which ₹6 per share has been called and paid. The dividend payable to her is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 51 — dividend in proportion to the amount paid-up

readLink.label: Read: Calls, advances and proportionate dividend →

options.explanation: That computes 12% on the NOMINAL value (5,000 × ₹10). Under a s. 51 article the base is the paid-up amount of ₹6 per share.
That computes 12% on the UNPAID ₹4 per share. Dividend is paid on what has been paid up, not on what remains uncalled.
Correct. 5,000 shares × ₹6 paid-up × 12% = ₹3,600 — the article shifts the dividend base from nominal value to the amount paid-up.
That takes 12% on ₹8 per share, splitting the difference between nominal and paid-up. Section 51 fixes the base at the amount actually paid-up, here ₹6.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 52 · Uses of securities premium
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a permitted application of the securities premium account under section 52(2) of the Companies Act 2013?

readLink.label: Read: Securities premium, discount and sweat equity →

options.text: Issuing fully paid bonus shares to members out of unissued shares
options.explanation: Expressly permitted by s. 52(2)(a).

options.text: Writing off the preliminary expenses of the company
options.explanation: Expressly permitted by s. 52(2)(b).

options.text: Providing for the premium payable on the redemption of redeemable preference shares or debentures
options.explanation: Expressly permitted by s. 52(2)(d).

options.text: Paying an interim dividend to equity shareholders in a year of inadequate profits
options.explanation: Correct. This use is not in the list. The premium account is treated like paid-up capital, not a distributable reserve; dividend can never be paid out of it.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 52 · Nature of the premium account
questions.stem: The securities premium account of Charaiveti Textiles Limited stands at ₹60 lakh. Which statement about the account is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Securities premium, discount and sweat equity →

options.text: The provisions of the Act relating to reduction of share capital apply as if the account were paid-up share capital, so it can be applied outside the section 52 list only through a reduction under section 66
options.explanation: Correct. Section 52(2) applies the reduction discipline to the premium account; outside the five listed applications (and s. 68 buy-back), leaving the account means a s. 66 reduction with Tribunal confirmation.

options.text: It is a free reserve which may be distributed as dividend by ordinary resolution
options.explanation: The premium account is quasi-capital, not a free reserve for distribution — dividend from it is never permitted. (Only for the s. 68 buy-back ceilings does an Explanation treat it as included in free reserves.)

options.text: It may be used to write off accumulated trading losses
options.explanation: Trading losses are not in the s. 52(2) list; writing them off against the premium account would need a s. 66 reduction.

options.text: It must be transferred to the capital redemption reserve within one year of the issue
options.explanation: No such transfer exists. The CRR arises on redemption of preference shares out of profits (s. 55) and on buy-back (s. 69), not from the premium account by lapse of time.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 53 · Prohibition of issue at discount
questions.stem: Mahodadhi Shipping Limited, with the approval of its shareholders by special resolution, issues equity shares at a discount of 8% to a strategic investor. The legal position is:

readLink.label: Read: Securities premium, discount and sweat equity →

options.text: The issue is valid because a special resolution authorised it
options.explanation: No resolution can authorise what s. 53 prohibits. The only doors are sweat equity under s. 54 and the s. 53(2A) conversion of debt into shares under an RBI-guided plan.

options.text: The shares are void; the company and every officer in default face a penalty which may extend to the amount raised through the issue or ₹5 lakh, whichever is less, and the company must refund all monies received with interest at 12% per annum from the date of issue
options.explanation: Correct. Section 53(2) makes the discounted shares void, and s. 53(3) stacks the capped penalty and the 12% refund obligation on top.

options.text: The issue is valid if an intimation is filed with the Registrar within 30 days
options.explanation: No filing cures a discounted issue; the prohibition is absolute outside ss. 54 and 53(2A).

options.text: The issue is voidable at the option of the allottee
options.explanation: The shares are VOID, not voidable — neither the company nor the allottee can elect to keep them alive.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 53(3) · Refund with 12% interest
questions.stem: Kaustubh Forgings Limited issued 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹9 per share on 1 May 2026, receiving ₹4,50,000. The contravention of section 53 is established and the monies are refunded on 1 January 2027, exactly eight months after the date of issue. The interest payable under section 53(3) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 53(3) — refund with interest at 12% per annum from the date of issue

readLink.label: Read: Securities premium, discount and sweat equity →

options.explanation: Correct. ₹4,50,000 × 12% × 8/12 = ₹36,000 — interest runs at 12% per annum from the DATE OF ISSUE to the refund, here eight months.
That is a full year's interest (₹4,50,000 × 12%). The shares were outstanding for only eight months.
That computes nine months of interest. The period from 1 May 2026 to 1 January 2027 is eight months.
That is six months of interest. The refund came eight months, not six, after the date of issue.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 54 · Sweat equity conditions
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for the issue of sweat equity shares under section 54 of the Companies Act 2013, as it now stands?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 54(1) — the one-year condition stands omitted by amendment

readLink.label: Read: Securities premium, discount and sweat equity →

options.text: A special resolution specifying the number of shares, the current market price, the consideration, if any, and the class or classes of directors or employees to whom the shares are to be issued
options.explanation: This is the core s. 54(1)(b) requirement — the special resolution must carry these four particulars.

options.text: The sweat equity shares must be of a class of shares already issued
options.explanation: Section 54(1)(a) requires this; a company cannot create a brand-new class through a sweat-equity issue.

options.text: For listed equity shares, compliance with the SEBI regulations governing sweat equity
options.explanation: Section 54(1)(d) sends listed issues to the SEBI regulations and unlisted issues to the prescribed rules.

options.text: At least one year must have elapsed since the date on which the company commenced business
options.explanation: Correct. This is NOT a requirement any more. The one-year condition was omitted by amendment, so even a newly incorporated company may issue sweat equity. Older material still lists it; treat it as a named trap.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 55 · Tenure of preference shares
questions.stem: Under section 55 of the Companies Act 2013, a company limited by shares may issue redeemable preference shares for a period:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, ss. 55(1)–(2) and proviso; rules-level infrastructure tenure

readLink.label: Read: Preference shares and their redemption →

options.text: Not exceeding ten years from the date of issue, in all cases
options.explanation: The general ceiling is twenty years, not ten.

options.text: Of any length, including irredeemable preference shares, if the articles authorise it
options.explanation: Section 55(1) prohibits irredeemable preference shares outright; the articles cannot override the statute.

options.text: Not exceeding twenty years from the date of issue — except that for infrastructure projects a longer period may be allowed (rules-level: up to thirty years), subject to the prescribed minimum annual redemption at the option of the holders
options.explanation: Correct. Twenty years is the s. 55(2) ceiling; the infrastructure carve-out and its thirty-year outer limit with annual redemption sit in the rules and are amendment-sensitive.

options.text: Not exceeding thirty years from the date of issue, for every company
options.explanation: Thirty years is only the rules-level outer limit for infrastructure projects; the general ceiling is twenty years.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 55(2) · Redemption preconditions
questions.stem: Which statement about the redemption of preference shares under section 55(2) is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Preference shares and their redemption →

options.text: Preference shares may be redeemed out of any reserve, including the revaluation reserve, if the articles permit
options.explanation: The sources are closed: profits which would otherwise be available for dividend, or the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purposes of the redemption. A revaluation reserve is neither.

options.text: Only fully paid preference shares may be redeemed, and only out of profits available for dividend or out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purposes of the redemption
options.explanation: Correct. Both provisos operate together — the fully-paid precondition and the two exclusive sources.

options.text: Preference shares may be redeemed out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of debentures
options.explanation: The proviso speaks of a fresh issue of SHARES made for the purposes of the redemption; debenture proceeds are borrowings, not share proceeds.

options.text: Partly paid preference shares may be redeemed to the extent of the amount paid-up
options.explanation: No pro tanto redemption exists — the shares must be fully paid before any redemption; the company must first call the balance.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 55 · Capital Redemption Reserve
questions.stem: Amoghavarsha Chemicals Limited redeems 2,00,000 preference shares of ₹100 each, fully paid, at par. For the purposes of the redemption it makes a fresh issue of equity shares with proceeds of ₹80,00,000, and meets the balance out of profits otherwise available for dividend. The amount to be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 55(2)(c) — CRR equal to the nominal amount redeemed out of profits

readLink.label: Read: Preference shares and their redemption →

options.explanation: That transfers the whole nominal amount, ignoring the fresh issue. The CRR equals only the nominal amount redeemed OUT OF PROFITS — the slice funded by fresh-issue proceeds is already replaced by new capital.
Correct. Nominal amount redeemed = ₹2,00,00,000; funded by fresh issue = ₹80,00,000; redeemed out of profits = ₹1,20,00,000, and that sum goes to the CRR.
That is the fresh-issue slice — precisely the part which needs NO CRR, because new capital has replaced the redeemed capital.

options.text: Nil
options.explanation: A CRR is dispensable only where the WHOLE redemption is funded by a fresh issue. Here ₹1,20,00,000 came out of profits, and that amount must be capitalised in the CRR.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 55(2)(d) · Premium on redemption
questions.stem: The premium payable on the redemption of preference shares must be provided:

readLink.label: Read: Preference shares and their redemption →

options.text: Out of the profits of the company or out of the securities premium account, before the shares are redeemed — and, for the prescribed class of companies whose financial statements comply with the section 133 accounting standards, out of profits only
options.explanation: Correct. Section 55(2)(d) requires provision BEFORE redemption, from profits or the securities premium account, with the narrower profits-only rule for the AS-compliant class (amendment-sensitive).

options.text: Out of the Capital Redemption Reserve account
options.explanation: The CRR receives the nominal amount redeemed out of profits and flows out only into fully paid bonus shares; the premium never touches it.

options.text: Out of the proceeds of the fresh issue of shares made for the redemption
options.explanation: Fresh-issue proceeds fund the CAPITAL portion of the redemption; the premium must come from profits or the securities premium account.

options.text: At any time within one year after the redemption
options.explanation: The provision must be made BEFORE the shares are redeemed; there is no one-year grace.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 56(1) · Delivery of the instrument of transfer
questions.stem: An instrument of transfer of shares in Form SH-4, relating to shares of Devagiri Foods Private Limited, is duly executed on 10 April 2026. To be registrable under section 56(1), the instrument, along with the share certificate, must be delivered to the company by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 56(1) — instrument delivered within 60 days from the date of execution

readLink.label: Read: Transfer and transmission — ss. 56 to 59 →

options.explanation: That is 30 days. The s. 56(1) period is 60 days from the date of execution — 30 days is the s. 58 refusal-notice clock, a different provision.

options.text: 10 June 2026
options.explanation: That reads the period as two calendar months. Section 56(1) counts 60 DAYS from execution, which lands on 9 June 2026.

options.text: 9 July 2026
options.explanation: That is 90 days. The statutory period is 60 days from the date of execution.

options.text: 9 June 2026
options.explanation: Correct. 60 days from 10 April 2026 (20 days of April + 31 of May + 9 of June) expires on 9 June 2026. Late delivery leaves registration to the Board's indemnity discretion under the proviso.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 56(4) · Certificate-delivery timelines
questions.stem: Which of the following certificate-delivery timelines under section 56(4) of the Companies Act 2013 is CORRECTLY stated?

readLink.label: Read: Transfer and transmission — ss. 56 to 59 →

options.text: Certificates for shares allotted — within six months from the date of allotment
options.explanation: Share certificates on allotment are due within TWO months of allotment; six months is the debenture timeline.

options.text: Certificates on a transfer — within two months from the date of receipt of the instrument of transfer
options.explanation: The transfer and transmission timeline is ONE month from receipt of the instrument or intimation, not two.

options.text: Certificates for debentures allotted — within six months from the date of allotment
options.explanation: Correct. Debenture certificates get the longest clock: six months from allotment. Shares get two months (incorporation or allotment) and one month (transfer or transmission receipt).

options.text: Certificates to subscribers to the memorandum — within one month from the date of incorporation
options.explanation: Subscribers' certificates are due within TWO months of incorporation.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 56 · Transmission of shares
questions.stem: On the death of Dhanvantri, his shares in Ketaki Ceramics Limited devolve on his son as legal heir, who applies to be registered as a member. Which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, ss. 56(1)–(2) — transmission by operation of law

readLink.label: Read: Transfer and transmission — ss. 56 to 59 →

options.text: This is a transmission by operation of law; no instrument of transfer in Form SH-4 and no stamp duty are required, and the company registers the son on an intimation of transmission with proof of entitlement
options.explanation: Correct. Transmission is devolution by operation of law (death, insolvency, lunacy); the s. 56(1) instrument-of-transfer machinery does not apply, and the certificate follows within one month of receipt of the intimation.

options.text: The son must execute Form SH-4 jointly with the legal representatives of the deceased and pay stamp duty
options.explanation: Form SH-4 belongs to a voluntary TRANSFER. A transmission needs only intimation and proof; no execution, no stamp duty.

options.text: Registration requires an order of the Tribunal in every case of transmission
options.explanation: The Tribunal enters only on a refusal (s. 58) or a rectification dispute (s. 59); routine transmission is registered by the company itself.

options.text: The shares vest in the company until probate is produced
options.explanation: Shares never vest in the company on a member's death; they devolve on the legal representative, and the company's role is to register the devolution on proper proof.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 58 · Private-company refusal and appeal
questions.stem: Nalanda Traders Private Limited receives a duly executed instrument of transfer on 4 August 2026 and its Board decides to refuse registration. Which statement correctly sets out the section 58 position?

readLink.label: Read: Transfer and transmission — ss. 56 to 59 →

options.text: The company must send notice of the refusal within 15 days of delivery of the instrument
options.explanation: The refusal notice must go within 30 days of delivery, not 15.

options.text: The transferee may appeal to the Tribunal within 90 days of receipt of the refusal notice
options.explanation: Ninety days belongs to the PUBLIC-company no-notice situation. For a private company the appeal windows are 30 days (notice received) and 60 days (no notice).

options.text: A private company need not send any notice of refusal, since its articles restrict transfers
options.explanation: The restriction in the articles justifies the refusal, but s. 58(1) still compels a reasoned notice of refusal within 30 days.

options.text: The company must send notice of the refusal, with reasons, within 30 days of the date the instrument was delivered; the transferee may appeal to the Tribunal within 30 days of receipt of the notice or, where no notice is sent, within 60 days of the date the instrument was delivered
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the three private-company clocks under ss. 58(1) and 58(3): 30 days for the notice, then 30 or 60 days for the appeal depending on whether notice was sent.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 58 · Public-company transferability
questions.stem: Which statement about the transfer of securities of a PUBLIC company under section 58 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Transfer and transmission — ss. 56 to 59 →

options.text: A public company may refuse any transfer at its discretion, like a private company
options.explanation: Section 58(2) makes the securities of a public company FREELY transferable; a refusal must rest on sufficient cause.

options.text: The securities of a public company are freely transferable; on a refusal without sufficient cause, the transferee may appeal to the Tribunal within 60 days of receipt of the refusal notice or, where no notice is sent, within 90 days of delivery of the instrument of transfer
options.explanation: Correct. Free transferability is the rule, and the public-company appeal windows are 60 and 90 days under s. 58(4).

options.text: The appeal against a refusal lies to the Regional Director
options.explanation: The appeal lies to the TRIBUNAL, which may order registration within ten days of its order or direct rectification with damages.

options.text: A contract between two persons with respect to the transfer of securities is void as a fetter on free transferability
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 58(2) says the opposite: such a contract or arrangement is enforceable as a contract.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 59 · Rectification of the register
questions.stem: Where the name of a person is, without sufficient cause, entered in or omitted from the register of members of a company, the remedy of rectification lies before:

readLink.label: Read: Transfer and transmission — ss. 56 to 59 →

options.text: The Registrar of Companies
options.explanation: The Registrar keeps the public registry of filings; rectification of the company's register of MEMBERS is a Tribunal matter.

options.text: The Central Government
options.explanation: The Central Government has no rectification role under s. 59.

options.text: The Tribunal — or a competent court outside India, specified by the Central Government, where the applicant is a member or debenture-holder residing outside India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 59(1) routes the aggrieved person, any member, or the company to the Tribunal, with the foreign-forum alternative for persons resident outside India.

options.text: The civil court alone, rectification being a question of title
options.explanation: Section 59 gives the Tribunal the rectification jurisdiction; the aggrieved person is not confined to a civil suit.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 61 · Modes needing Tribunal approval
questions.stem: Which of the following alterations of share capital under section 61(1) takes effect only with the approval of the Tribunal?

readLink.label: Read: Alteration of share capital — ss. 61 and 64 →

options.text: A consolidation and division of share capital which results in changes in the voting percentage of shareholders
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 61(1)(b) requires Tribunal approval for exactly this case; every other s. 61 mode needs only an ordinary resolution backed by the articles.

options.text: An increase of the authorised share capital
options.explanation: An increase needs only an ordinary resolution (articles permitting) and a s. 64 notice — no Tribunal.

options.text: A sub-division of shares into shares of a smaller amount
options.explanation: Sub-division needs no Tribunal; the only statutory condition is that the paid-unpaid proportion on each reduced share stays the same.

options.text: A cancellation of shares not taken or agreed to be taken by any person
options.explanation: Cancellation of unissued shares needs no Tribunal, and s. 61(2) declares it is not even a reduction of capital.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 61(2) and 64 · Cancellation of unissued shares
questions.stem: Trinayani Foods Limited, authorised by its articles, resolves to cancel 1,00,000 equity shares which have not been taken or agreed to be taken by any person, and to diminish its authorised capital by that amount. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Alteration of share capital — ss. 61 and 64 →

options.text: This is a reduction of share capital requiring confirmation by the Tribunal under section 66
options.explanation: Section 61(2) says the opposite: a cancellation of unissued shares is NOT deemed a reduction of share capital, so the s. 66 machinery never engages.

options.text: A special resolution is required for the cancellation
options.explanation: All s. 61 alterations, including this one, need only an ORDINARY resolution where the articles authorise the alteration.

options.text: The consent of every creditor must first be obtained
options.explanation: Creditor protection belongs to a s. 66 reduction. Cancelling shares nobody ever took returns nothing to anyone, so no creditor process applies.

options.text: An ordinary resolution suffices; the cancellation is expressly not a reduction of share capital, and notice of the alteration must be given to the Registrar within 30 days under section 64
options.explanation: Correct. Ordinary resolution (articles permitting), s. 61(2) takes it outside reduction, and s. 64 requires the 30-day notice with the altered memorandum.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 62(1)(a) · Rights-offer window
questions.stem: Chitradurga Cements Limited makes a rights offer to its equity shareholders by a letter of offer dated 1 September 2026. Ignoring any shorter period prescribed under the rules, the LATEST date up to which the offer may remain open under section 62(1)(a)(i) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 62(1)(a)(i) — offer open not less than 15 and not more than 30 days from the date of the offer

readLink.label: Read: Further issue of capital — s. 62 →

options.text: 16 September 2026
options.explanation: That is 15 days from the date of the offer — the EARLIEST lawful closing date, not the latest.

options.text: 1 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. The offer cannot remain open beyond 30 days from the date of the offer: 30 days from 1 September 2026 runs out on 1 October 2026. If not accepted by the closing date, the offer is deemed declined.

options.text: 31 October 2026
options.explanation: That is 60 days from the date of the offer. The statutory ceiling is 30 days.

options.text: 1 November 2026
options.explanation: That reads the ceiling as two calendar months. Section 62(1)(a)(i) counts 30 DAYS from the date of the offer.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 62(1)(a) · Renunciation and deemed decline
questions.stem: A rights offer under section 62(1)(a) is made to Charudatta, an equity shareholder, who neither accepts the offer nor renounces it within the offer period. The position is:

readLink.label: Read: Further issue of capital — s. 62 →

options.text: The offer remains open until Charudatta expressly rejects it in writing
options.explanation: The notice itself fixes the period; on its expiry without acceptance, the offer is DEEMED to have been declined — no express rejection is needed.

options.text: The unaccepted shares stand cancelled and reduce the authorised capital
options.explanation: Nothing is cancelled. The shares remain available for the Board to place.

options.text: The offer is deemed to have been declined, and the Board may dispose of the shares in such manner, not disadvantageous to the shareholders and the company, as it thinks fit
options.explanation: Correct. Deemed decline on expiry, then Board disposal under s. 62(1)(a)(iii) subject to the not-disadvantageous standard. Charudatta could instead have renounced in favour of any person, unless the articles provide otherwise.

options.text: The shares must be offered to the public through a prospectus
options.explanation: No compulsory public offer follows; the Board's disposal power is general, bounded only by the not-disadvantageous condition.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 62(1)(b)–(c) · ESOP and preferential allotment
questions.stem: Which statement about further issues of shares under section 62 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Further issue of capital — s. 62 →

options.text: An issue to employees under a scheme of employees' stock option requires a special resolution, and an issue to any other persons under section 62(1)(c) requires a special resolution with the price determined by the valuation report of a registered valuer
options.explanation: Correct. ESOP needs a special resolution (a private company may pass an ordinary resolution under its exemption notification), and the preferential route needs a special resolution plus registered-valuer pricing.

options.text: An ESOP issue may be made by a Board resolution alone in every company
options.explanation: The section requires a special resolution for ESOP; only a private company is let down to an ordinary resolution by exemption notification — never to a Board resolution alone.

options.text: The price for a preferential allotment is determined by a merchant banker's certificate
options.explanation: Section 62(1)(c) names the REGISTERED VALUER's valuation report as the pricing anchor.

options.text: A rights issue under section 62(1)(a) requires a special resolution of the members
options.explanation: A rights issue to existing holders in proportion needs no members' resolution at all — the Board makes the offer.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 63 · Sources for bonus shares
questions.stem: Out of which of the following can a company NOT issue fully paid bonus shares under section 63?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 63(1) and its proviso

readLink.label: Read: Bonus shares — s. 63 →

options.text: Its free reserves
options.explanation: Free reserves head the s. 63(1) list of permitted sources.

options.text: The securities premium account
options.explanation: Expressly permitted by s. 63(1)(ii), and consistent with s. 52(2)(a).

options.text: The capital redemption reserve account
options.explanation: Expressly permitted by s. 63(1)(iii) — bonus shares are the CRR's only outward application.

options.text: Reserves created by the revaluation of assets
options.explanation: Correct. This is the prohibited source. The proviso to s. 63(1) bars capitalising unrealised revaluation surpluses into bonus shares.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 63 · Amount available for capitalisation
questions.stem: The balance sheet of Suparna Textiles Limited shows: free reserves ₹32,00,000; securities premium account ₹10,00,000; capital redemption reserve ₹8,00,000; and a reserve created on the revaluation of assets ₹12,00,000. The maximum amount the company may capitalise for an issue of fully paid bonus shares under section 63 is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 63(1) — free reserves, securities premium and CRR; never the revaluation reserve

readLink.label: Read: Bonus shares — s. 63 →

options.explanation: That adds the revaluation reserve of ₹12,00,000, which the proviso to s. 63(1) expressly excludes from bonus capitalisation.
That takes free reserves and securities premium but drops the CRR of ₹8,00,000, which s. 63(1)(iii) expressly permits.
Correct. Free reserves ₹32,00,000 + securities premium ₹10,00,000 + CRR ₹8,00,000 = ₹50,00,000; the revaluation reserve of ₹12,00,000 can never be used.
That confines the bonus to free reserves alone; the securities premium account and the CRR are equally permitted sources.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 63(2) · Conditions for a bonus issue
questions.stem: Which statement about the conditions for a bonus issue is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 63(2) and rules-level conditions

readLink.label: Read: Bonus shares — s. 63 →

options.text: Bonus shares may be issued in lieu of the dividend for the year
options.explanation: The rules-level condition prohibits exactly this: bonus shares cannot substitute for dividend.

options.text: Any partly paid-up shares outstanding must be made fully paid-up before the bonus issue, and a Board recommendation of a bonus issue, once announced, cannot be withdrawn
options.explanation: Correct. Section 63(2)(e) requires partly paid shares to be made fully paid first, and the rules bar withdrawal of an announced recommendation.

options.text: A bonus issue is permitted even where the company has defaulted in depositing employees' provident fund contributions
options.explanation: Section 63(2)(d) bars a bonus while there is default in payment of statutory dues of employees such as provident fund, gratuity and bonus.

options.text: A bonus issue requires the confirmation of the Tribunal
options.explanation: No Tribunal enters a bonus issue: the requirements are the articles, a general-meeting authorisation on the Board's recommendation, and the no-default conditions.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 66 · Reduction of share capital
questions.stem: Which statement about the reduction of share capital under section 66 is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 66(1) and its proviso

readLink.label: Read: Reduction of share capital — s. 66 →

options.text: It requires a special resolution and confirmation by the Tribunal, and no reduction may be made if the company is in arrears in the repayment of any deposits accepted by it, or the interest payable thereon
options.explanation: Correct. Both the double approval (special resolution + NCLT confirmation) and the deposit-arrears bar come straight from s. 66(1) and its proviso.

options.text: It requires only an ordinary resolution filed with the Registrar
options.explanation: Reduction is the most heavily guarded capital alteration: special resolution AND Tribunal confirmation, with notice to the Central Government, Registrar, SEBI (listed) and creditors.

options.text: A company in arrears on deposits may reduce its capital if the arrears are secured
options.explanation: The proviso is absolute — deposit or deposit-interest arrears bar the reduction; security does not lift the bar.

options.text: A buy-back under section 68 also requires the Tribunal's confirmation under section 66
options.explanation: Section 66(6) says the section does not apply to a s. 68 buy-back, which is a self-contained code with no Tribunal role.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 66 vs 68 · Reduction versus buy-back
questions.stem: Which of the following CORRECTLY distinguishes a reduction of share capital under section 66 from a buy-back under section 68?

readLink.label: Read: Reduction of share capital — s. 66 →

options.text: Both require the confirmation of the Tribunal
options.explanation: Only the s. 66 reduction goes to the Tribunal; a buy-back never does.

options.text: A buy-back may be funded out of any reserve, including the revaluation reserve
options.explanation: Buy-back sources are closed — free reserves, the securities premium account, or the proceeds of an earlier issue of a different kind of security.

options.text: A reduction is limited to 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves
options.explanation: The 25% ceiling belongs to buy-back; a s. 66 reduction has no percentage cap — the Tribunal process is the control.

options.text: A reduction requires Tribunal confirmation with creditor protection built into the process, whereas a buy-back proceeds without Tribunal approval, subject instead to the statutory ceilings, the declaration of solvency and the post-buy-back debt cap
options.explanation: Correct. That is the structural contrast: judicial confirmation and creditor hearings on one side; self-executing ceilings, solvency declaration and the 2:1 debt cap on the other.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 67 · Financial assistance
questions.stem: Which of the following financial assistance is PERMITTED to a public company under section 67?

readLink.label: Read: Buy-back and restrictions — ss. 67 to 70 →

options.text: A guarantee to enable a promoter to purchase shares of the company
options.explanation: Assistance to a promoter for purchasing the company's own shares is squarely within the s. 67(2) prohibition.

options.text: A loan to an employee, not being a director or key managerial personnel, of an amount not exceeding six months' salary or wages, to enable him to purchase fully paid shares of the company to be held by way of beneficial ownership
options.explanation: Correct. Section 67(3)(c) carves out exactly this employee loan — capped at six months' salary or wages, for fully paid shares, beneficially held, and never for directors or KMP.

options.text: An interest-free loan to a director to subscribe to a rights issue
options.explanation: Directors and key managerial personnel are expressly outside the employee-loan exception.

options.text: A loan to its subsidiary to purchase the company's shares from the market
options.explanation: Routing the assistance through a subsidiary is still indirect financial assistance for the purchase of its own shares — prohibited (and s. 70 separately bars buy-back through subsidiaries).

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 68(2) · Buy-back ceilings
questions.stem: Regarding the ceilings on a buy-back under section 68(2), which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 68(2)(b)–(c) and Explanation II

readLink.label: Read: Buy-back and restrictions — ss. 67 to 70 →

options.text: A buy-back of equity shares in any financial year is limited to 25% of the free reserves
options.explanation: The financial-year proviso applies the 25% to the total PAID-UP EQUITY CAPITAL, not to free reserves.

options.text: The 25% ceiling is computed on paid-up capital and free reserves excluding the securities premium account
options.explanation: Explanation II to s. 68 makes free reserves INCLUDE the securities premium account for buy-back purposes, so the premium enters the base.

options.text: The buy-back must not exceed 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves (free reserves including the securities premium account), and a buy-back of equity shares in any financial year must not exceed 25% of the total paid-up equity capital in that financial year
options.explanation: Correct. Both 25% tests operate together — the amount test on the aggregate base and the equity test on paid-up equity capital — and every share bought back must be fully paid.

options.text: The Board alone may authorise a buy-back of up to 20% of paid-up capital and free reserves
options.explanation: The Board route stops at 10% of the paid-up equity capital and free reserves; anything more needs a special resolution.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 68 · Buy-back timelines and filings
questions.stem: Which statement about the procedure and timelines for a buy-back under section 68 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Buy-back and restrictions — ss. 67 to 70 →

options.text: The securities bought back must be extinguished and physically destroyed within 7 days of the last date of completion of the buy-back, and a return of buy-back must be filed with the Registrar (and SEBI, for a listed company) within 30 days of completion
options.explanation: Correct. Seven days for extinguishment (s. 68(7)) and thirty days for the SH-11 return (s. 68(10)); completion itself must fall within one year of the resolution, and no fresh buy-back offer may be made within one year of the closure of the preceding offer.

options.text: Extinguishment of the bought-back securities may be done within 30 days of completion
options.explanation: Thirty days is the return-filing clock; extinguishment and physical destruction must happen within SEVEN days of the last date of completion.

options.text: A further issue of the same kind of shares may be made one month after the buy-back
options.explanation: The cooling-off is SIX months, subject to the exceptions for bonus shares and the discharge of subsisting obligations such as conversions, stock options and sweat equity.

options.text: The buy-back must be completed within two years of the date of the special resolution
options.explanation: Completion must come within ONE year of the special resolution (or the Board resolution on the 10% route).

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 70 · Prohibited buy-backs
questions.stem: Bharadwaj Auto Limited defaulted in the repayment of a term loan to its bank; the default was fully remedied on 31 March 2024. The company also has a wholly owned investment-company subsidiary. Which statement about a proposed buy-back is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 70(1) and its proviso

readLink.label: Read: Buy-back and restrictions — ss. 67 to 70 →

options.text: The company may route the buy-back through its investment-company subsidiary
options.explanation: Section 70(1)(a)–(b) prohibits a buy-back through ANY subsidiary or through any investment company — the route is barred absolutely.

options.text: The buy-back became permissible immediately when the default was remedied
options.explanation: The proviso adds a waiting period: the default must be remedied AND three years must have lapsed after it ceased to subsist.

options.text: Having once defaulted, the company can never buy back its shares
options.explanation: The bar is not perpetual — it lifts once the default is remedied and three years have passed since it ceased to subsist.

options.text: A direct buy-back is prohibited until three years have lapsed after the default ceased to subsist (that is, until 31 March 2027), and a buy-back through any subsidiary or investment company is prohibited absolutely
options.explanation: Correct. The default-based bar runs to the third anniversary of the remedy, and the structural prohibitions on subsidiaries and investment companies admit no exception. Compliance with ss. 92, 123, 127 and 129 is a further precondition.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Case: sizing a buy-back against every ceiling
questions.case: The audited balance sheet of Arunodaya Precision Limited as at 31 March 2026 shows: paid-up equity share capital ₹1,00,00,000 (10,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully paid); free reserves ₹2,20,00,000; securities premium account ₹80,00,000; secured loans ₹5,00,00,000; and unsecured loans ₹2,60,00,000. There is no preference capital, no subsisting default of the kind described in section 70, and the articles authorise buy-back. The Board proposes to buy back 2,50,000 equity shares at ₹40 per share, an outflow of ₹1,00,00,000, funded out of free reserves.

readLink.label: Read: Buy-back and restrictions — ss. 67 to 70 →

questions.stem: The maximum amount of buy-back the company may undertake with the authority of a special resolution under section 68(2)(b) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 68(2)(b) and Explanation II — 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves, free reserves including the securities premium account

options.explanation: That takes 25% of ₹3,20,00,000, excluding the securities premium. Explanation II to s. 68 includes the securities premium account in free reserves for buy-back purposes, so the base is ₹4,00,00,000.
That is 25% of the paid-up capital alone. The ceiling is 25% of the AGGREGATE of paid-up capital and free reserves (including securities premium).
Correct. Base = ₹1,00,00,000 + ₹2,20,00,000 + ₹80,00,000 = ₹4,00,00,000; 25% of the base = ₹1,00,00,000. The proposed outflow sits exactly at the ceiling, so it needs the special-resolution route.
That is the 10% BOARD-resolution ceiling, not the special-resolution ceiling of 25%.

questions.stem: If the Board wished to proceed WITHOUT a special resolution, by a resolution of the Board alone, the maximum buy-back permitted is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, first proviso to s. 68(2) — Board route up to 10% of paid-up equity capital and free reserves

options.explanation: Correct. The Board route runs to 10% of the paid-up equity capital and free reserves (including securities premium): 10% of ₹4,00,00,000 = ₹40,00,000. The proposed ₹1,00,00,000 buy-back therefore cannot use this route.
That is 10% of the paid-up capital alone; the base also includes free reserves and the securities premium account.
That is the 25% special-resolution ceiling. The Board acting alone stops at 10%.
That is 10% of a base which wrongly excludes the securities premium account of ₹80,00,000.

questions.stem: Under section 68(2)(d), after the buy-back the aggregate of the company's secured and unsecured debts must not exceed twice its paid-up capital and free reserves. On the balance-sheet figures as they stand, that ceiling amounts to:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 68(2)(d) — post-buy-back debts not more than twice the paid-up capital and free reserves

options.explanation: That is the base itself (paid-up capital plus free reserves including premium), not twice the base.

Correct. Twice (₹1,00,00,000 + ₹2,20,00,000 + ₹80,00,000) = ₹8,00,00,000. The existing debts of ₹7,60,00,000 are within it on the opening figures, though the test must hold AFTER the buy-back reduces capital and reserves.
That is four times the base. The statutory multiple is two (the Central Government may notify a higher ratio only for prescribed classes).
That is the company's existing aggregate debt, the figure to be TESTED against the ceiling — not the ceiling itself.

questions.stem: The buy-back of 2,50,000 shares of ₹10 each at ₹40 per share is completed out of free reserves. The amount to be transferred to the capital redemption reserve account under section 69 is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 69(1) — CRR equal to the nominal value of the shares bought back

options.explanation: That is the full consideration paid (2,50,000 × ₹40). The CRR is created only for the NOMINAL value of the shares purchased.
That is the premium element of the consideration (₹30 per share). The premium never enters the CRR computation.

options.text: Nil
options.explanation: A buy-back out of free reserves (or securities premium) always requires the CRR transfer; only the extinguished nominal capital is being replaced by the reserve.
Correct. CRR = nominal value bought back = 2,50,000 × ₹10 = ₹25,00,000, disclosed in the balance sheet and available only for fully paid bonus shares.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Case: redeeming preference shares and building the CRR
questions.case: Meghdoot Agro Limited has 1,00,000 9% redeemable preference shares of ₹100 each, fully paid, falling due for redemption at a premium of 10%. Its balance sheet shows profits otherwise available for dividend of ₹75,00,000 and a securities premium account of ₹18,00,000. For the purposes of the redemption, the company makes a fresh issue of 40,000 equity shares of ₹100 each at par, realising proceeds of ₹40,00,000. The articles authorise everything proposed.

readLink.label: Read: Preference shares and their redemption →

questions.stem: Which statement about the legality of the proposed redemption is correct?

options.text: The redemption may be funded partly out of the revaluation reserve if profits fall short
options.explanation: The sources are closed — profits otherwise available for dividend, or the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purposes of the redemption. A revaluation reserve is neither.

options.text: The redemption may proceed because the shares are fully paid, and it may be funded only out of profits otherwise available for dividend or out of the proceeds of the fresh issue of shares made for the purposes of the redemption
options.explanation: Correct. The fully-paid precondition is satisfied, and the two-source rule of s. 55(2) governs the funding — here ₹40,00,000 of fresh-issue proceeds and the balance from distributable profits.

options.text: The proceeds of a fresh issue of debentures could equally be used
options.explanation: Debenture proceeds are borrowings. The proviso permits only the proceeds of a fresh issue of SHARES made for the purposes of the redemption.

options.text: The approval of the Tribunal is required before any preference shares are redeemed
options.explanation: A routine redemption needs no Tribunal. The NCLT enters only under s. 55(3), where a company UNABLE to redeem issues further preference shares with the consent of three-fourths in value.

questions.stem: The amount to be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve account on the redemption is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 55(2)(c) — a sum equal to the nominal amount redeemed out of profits

options.explanation: That capitalises the entire nominal amount, ignoring that ₹40,00,000 of the redemption is funded by the fresh issue, which itself replaces the redeemed capital.
That is the fresh-issue slice — the one part of the redemption that needs NO CRR.
Correct. Nominal amount ₹1,00,00,000 less fresh-issue proceeds ₹40,00,000 = ₹60,00,000 redeemed out of profits, and that sum must go to the CRR.
That adds the 10% premium of ₹10,00,000. The CRR is computed on the NOMINAL value alone; the premium is provided separately out of profits or the securities premium account.

questions.stem: As to the premium of ₹10,00,000 payable on the redemption, and the use of the Capital Redemption Reserve thereafter, which statement is correct?

options.text: The premium must be provided before the redemption, out of the profits of the company or out of the securities premium account; and the CRR may thereafter be applied only in paying up unissued shares to be issued to members as fully paid bonus shares
options.explanation: Correct. Section 55(2)(d) fixes the timing (before redemption) and the sources (profits or securities premium — profits only for the prescribed AS-compliant class); s. 55(4) confines the CRR's outward application to fully paid bonus shares.

options.text: The premium is provided out of the Capital Redemption Reserve created on the redemption
options.explanation: The CRR is built AFTER the redemption logic runs and receives only the nominal amount redeemed out of profits; the premium never comes out of it.

options.text: The premium must be met out of the proceeds of the fresh issue
options.explanation: Fresh-issue proceeds fund the capital portion; the premium comes from profits or the securities premium account.

options.text: The CRR may later be written back and distributed to members as dividend
options.explanation: The reduction-of-capital discipline applies to the CRR as if it were paid-up capital — distributing it as dividend would be an unconfirmed reduction. Its only application is fully paid bonus shares.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Case: a secured debenture issue to 620 persons
questions.case: Chandrahas Polymers Limited, a manufacturer (not an infrastructure company), issues secured, non-convertible debentures on 1 July 2026 by an offer made to 620 identified persons comprising its members and certain outside investors. The debentures carry a fixed coupon, and the terms of issue are silent on voting. One investor asks whether the debentures give him a say at general meetings, and another asks what happens if the company fails to redeem on maturity.

readLink.label: Read: Debentures and nomination — ss. 71 and 72 →

questions.stem: As to the appointment of a debenture trustee, the correct position is:

options.text: No trustee is required because the issue is not made through a prospectus to the public
options.explanation: Section 71(5) is triggered by a prospectus OR an offer or invitation to the public or to members exceeding five hundred persons — 620 offerees crosses the line even without a public prospectus.

options.text: A trustee may be appointed within sixty days after the allotment of the debentures
options.explanation: The trustee must be appointed BEFORE the issue of the prospectus or the making of the offer, not after allotment.

options.text: A trustee is required only where the debentures are listed on a stock exchange
options.explanation: Listing is irrelevant to s. 71(5); the trigger is the number of offerees exceeding five hundred.

options.text: Because the offer goes to more than five hundred persons, the company must appoint one or more debenture trustees before making the offer
options.explanation: Correct. An offer to 620 persons exceeds the 500-person threshold, so trustees must be in place before the offer, and the trustee's duty is to protect the debenture-holders' interests and redress their grievances.

questions.stem: Under the rules-level framework for secured debentures, the LATEST date by which these debentures must be redeemed is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules 2014 — secured debentures redeemable within 10 years from the date of issue (rules-level; infrastructure classes up to 30 years)

options.text: 1 July 2031
options.explanation: That is five years from issue. The rules-level ceiling for secured debentures of an ordinary company is ten years from the date of issue.

options.text: 1 July 2036
options.explanation: Correct. Ten years from the issue date of 1 July 2026 runs to 1 July 2036. The company is not in the infrastructure and other permitted classes that may stretch the tenure.

options.text: 1 July 2046
options.explanation: That is twenty years — the s. 55 ceiling for PREFERENCE SHARES, not the tenure limit for secured debentures.

options.text: 1 July 2056
options.explanation: Thirty years is available only to infrastructure companies and the other classes the rules permit; a polymer manufacturer is not among them.

questions.stem: As to the Debenture Redemption Reserve, which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 71(4); DRR percentages and exemptions are rules-level and amendment-sensitive

options.text: The DRR is created out of the profits of the company available for payment of dividend and is utilised only for the redemption of debentures; the percentage of the outstanding value, and the classes of companies wholly exempted, are rules-level and have been recast by amendment
options.explanation: Correct. Section 71(4) fixes the source (dividend-available profits) and the exclusive purpose (redemption); the quantum and the exemptions (listed issuers, NBFCs and others were carved out by a 2019 rules amendment) live in the rules — verify the current position for the attempt.

options.text: The DRR is created out of the securities premium account
options.explanation: The DRR must come out of PROFITS available for dividend; the securities premium account has its own closed list of uses under s. 52.

options.text: The DRR must always equal 100% of the value of the outstanding debentures
options.explanation: No 100% requirement exists; the prescribed percentage is rules-level (and several classes are wholly exempt).

options.text: The DRR requirement has been abolished for every company
options.explanation: The 2019 rules amendment exempted several classes, but the DRR obligation survives for the classes still covered — a blanket abolition overstates it.

questions.stem: On the two investors' questions — voting rights and the remedy on a failure to redeem — the correct position is:

options.text: The debenture-holders may vote at general meetings in proportion to the value of their holdings
options.explanation: Section 71(2) prohibits the issue of debentures carrying ANY voting rights; a debenture-holder is a creditor, not a member.

options.text: Nomination under section 72 is available for shares but not for debentures
options.explanation: Section 72 covers every holder of SECURITIES of a company, debentures included.

options.text: The debentures carry no voting rights; and if the company fails to redeem them on maturity or to pay interest when due, the Tribunal may, on the application of any or all of the debenture-holders or the debenture trustee, after hearing the parties, direct the company to redeem the debentures forthwith with payment of principal and interest
options.explanation: Correct. Section 71(2) bars voting rights outright, and s. 71(10) gives the NCLT the redeem-forthwith jurisdiction; default in complying with the order is separately punishable.

options.text: On default, the debenture trustee must itself redeem the debentures out of its own funds and recover from the company
options.explanation: No such obligation exists. The trustee protects the holders — including by petitioning the Tribunal under s. 71(9) or s. 71(10) — but never underwrites the redemption personally.

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 43, 47 and 48 · Kinds of capital, voting and class rights
questions.stem: State the kinds of share capital that a company limited by shares may have under section 43 of the Companies Act 2013. Explain the voting rights of equity and preference shareholders under section 47, and the manner in which the rights attached to a class of shares may be varied under section 48, including the remedy of dissenting shareholders. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 43: two kinds — equity share capital, which may be with voting rights or with differential rights as to dividend, voting or otherwise per the rules; and preference share capital, carrying a preferential right both to a dividend (fixed amount or fixed rate) and to repayment of capital on a winding up; capital that is not preference is residually equity

Differential voting rights are issued on rules-level conditions — authorisation in the articles, an ordinary resolution in general meeting (postal ballot where applicable), the prescribed ceiling of total voting power, and no subsisting defaults in filings, dividend, deposits or repayment obligations (amendment-sensitive)
skeleton.citation: Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules 2014 — DVR conditions

skeleton.point: Section 47(1): every equity member votes on every resolution, in proportion to his share of the paid-up equity capital

Section 47(2): a preference member votes only on resolutions directly affecting the rights attached to his preference shares — any resolution for winding up or for repayment or reduction of capital being deemed to affect them directly — but votes on EVERY resolution where the dividend on his class has remained unpaid for two years or more

Section 48(1): variation of class rights requires the written consent of holders of three-fourths of the issued shares of the class or a special resolution at a separate class meeting; where the variation affects the rights of another class, the consent of three-fourths of that other class is also required

Section 48(2): holders of not less than 10% of the issued shares of the class who did not consent or vote in favour may apply to the Tribunal within 21 days; the variation then has no effect unless and until confirmed by the Tribunal, whose decision is binding, and the order is filed with the Registrar within 30 days

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 52 to 54 · Premium, discount and sweat equity
questions.stem: Explain the manner in which the securities premium account may be applied under section 52 of the Companies Act 2013. State the consequences of an issue of shares at a discount under section 53, and the conditions on which a company may issue sweat equity shares under section 54. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 52(1)–(2): the aggregate premium is carried to the securities premium account, to which the reduction-of-capital provisions apply as if it were paid-up capital; it may be applied in (a) issuing fully paid bonus shares, (b) writing off preliminary expenses, (c) writing off the expenses of, commission paid or discount allowed on, an issue of shares or debentures, (d) providing the premium payable on redemption of redeemable preference shares or debentures, and (e) the buy-back of shares or other securities under section 68

Section 52(3): for the prescribed class of companies whose financial statements comply with the section 133 accounting standards, the premium may be applied only for bonus shares, writing off the expenses of or commission on an issue of equity shares, and buy-back under section 68
Section 53(1)–(2): except sweat equity under section 54, a company shall not issue shares at a discount, and any share issued at a discounted price is void

Section 53(2A): shares may be issued at a discount to creditors when debt is converted into shares in pursuance of a statutory resolution plan or debt-restructuring scheme in accordance with RBI guidelines or directions

Section 53(3): the company and every officer in default are liable to a penalty which may extend to the amount raised through the issue at a discount or ₹5 lakh, whichever is less, and the company must refund all monies received with interest at 12% per annum from the date of issue

Section 54: sweat equity shares must be of a class already issued; a special resolution must specify the number of shares, current market price, consideration (if any) and the class or classes of directors or employees; listed issues follow the SEBI regulations and unlisted issues the prescribed rules; the former one-year-from-commencement condition stands omitted by amendment

questions.topic: Ch 4 · s. 55 · Issue and redemption of preference shares
questions.stem: State the conditions subject to which a company limited by shares may issue and redeem preference shares under section 55 of the Companies Act 2013, explaining the Capital Redemption Reserve and the treatment of the premium payable on redemption. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 55(1)–(2): no irredeemable preference shares; issue only if authorised by the articles, redeemable within 20 years of issue — except that for infrastructure projects a longer period may be allowed (rules-level: up to 30 years, with the prescribed minimum annual redemption at the option of the holders)

Redemption preconditions: only fully paid preference shares may be redeemed, and only out of profits otherwise available for dividend or out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purposes of the redemption

CRR: where redemption is out of profits, a sum equal to the nominal amount of the shares redeemed is transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve, to which the reduction-of-capital provisions apply as if it were paid-up capital, and which may be applied only in paying up unissued shares as fully paid bonus shares; the premium on redemption is provided before redemption out of profits or the securities premium account (profits only, for the prescribed AS-compliant class)

Section 55(3): a company unable to redeem or pay the dividend due may, with the consent of holders of three-fourths in value and the approval of the Tribunal, issue further redeemable preference shares equal to the amount due, whereupon the unredeemed shares are deemed redeemed; the Tribunal must order immediate redemption for dissenters, and the further issue is not an increase of capital

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 56, 58 and 59 · Transfer and transmission
questions.stem: Describe the procedure for the transfer of shares under section 56 of the Companies Act 2013 and distinguish it from transmission. State the timelines for delivery of certificates under section 56(4), and the remedies available where a company refuses to register a transfer, for both private and public companies. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 56(1): registration only on a proper instrument of transfer in Form SH-4, duly stamped, dated and executed by or on behalf of transferor and transferee, delivered to the company within 60 days from the date of execution together with the certificate or allotment letter; where the instrument is lost or not delivered in time, the Board may register on such terms as to indemnity as it thinks fit
Partly paid shares: where the application is by the transferor alone, the company gives notice to the transferee in Form SH-5 and registers only if he raises no objection within two weeks of receipt

Transmission: devolution by operation of law (death, insolvency, lunacy); registered on an intimation of transmission with proof of entitlement — no instrument of transfer, no execution and no stamp duty

Section 56(4) timelines: certificates within 2 months of incorporation (subscribers), 2 months of allotment, 1 month of receipt of the instrument of transfer or intimation of transmission, and 6 months of allotment of debentures; for depository holdings the company intimates the depository immediately on allotment

Section 58: a private company refusing a transfer or transmission sends a reasoned notice within 30 days of delivery; appeal to the Tribunal within 30 days of the notice or 60 days of delivery where no notice. A public company's securities are freely transferable; appeal within 60 days of the notice or 90 days of delivery; the Tribunal may dismiss, order registration within 10 days of its order, or direct rectification with damages

Section 59: rectification of the register of members by the Tribunal (or the competent foreign court for persons resident outside India) where a name is entered or omitted without sufficient cause or with unnecessary delay

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 62 and 63 · Further issue and bonus shares
questions.stem: Explain the three routes by which a company may make a further issue of shares under section 62(1) of the Companies Act 2013, and the conditions for an issue of bonus shares under section 63. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 62(1)(a) — rights issue: offer to existing equity holders in proportion, as nearly as circumstances admit, to the paid-up capital on their shares, by notice specifying the number of shares and a period of not less than 15 and not more than 30 days from the date of the offer (or such lesser number of days as may be prescribed — rules-level), failing acceptance within which the offer is deemed declined

The offer includes a right of renunciation in favour of any other person unless the articles provide otherwise, and after the period expires or on earlier intimation of decline the Board may dispose of the shares in a manner not disadvantageous to the shareholders and the company

Section 62(1)(b) — ESOP: issue to employees under a scheme of employees' stock option, subject to a special resolution (ordinary resolution for a private company under its exemption notification) and the prescribed conditions; s. 62(1)(c) — preferential allotment to any persons, authorised by a special resolution, for cash or non-cash consideration, at a price determined by a registered valuer's valuation report
Section 63(1): bonus shares only out of free reserves, the securities premium account or the capital redemption reserve — and never out of reserves created by the revaluation of assets

Section 63(2) and rules: authorised by the articles and by the general meeting on the Board's recommendation; no subsisting default on deposits, debt securities or statutory dues of employees (provident fund, gratuity, bonus); partly paid shares made fully paid first; bonus never in lieu of dividend, and an announced recommendation cannot be withdrawn
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 63(2) and rules-level conditions

questions.topic: Ch 4 · ss. 68 to 70 · Buy-back of securities
questions.stem: State the sources from which, and the conditions subject to which, a company may buy back its own shares or other specified securities under section 68 of the Companies Act 2013. Explain the transfer to the capital redemption reserve under section 69 and the circumstances in which a buy-back is prohibited under section 70. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Sources: free reserves, the securities premium account, or the proceeds of an earlier issue of any shares or other specified securities — but never the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or securities; for the ceilings, free reserves include the securities premium account
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 68(1) and Explanation II

skeleton.point: Conditions: authorisation in the articles; a special resolution in general meeting, or a Board resolution alone where the buy-back is 10% or less of the paid-up equity capital and free reserves; the buy-back not exceeding 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves, and for equity shares in any financial year not exceeding 25% of the total paid-up equity capital; post-buy-back secured and unsecured debts not exceeding twice the paid-up capital and free reserves; and all securities bought back fully paid-up

Procedure and time limits: completion within one year of the resolution; no fresh offer of buy-back within one year of the closure of the preceding offer; declaration of solvency filed before the buy-back; extinguishment and physical destruction within 7 days of the last date of completion; no further issue of the same kind of securities within 6 months except bonus shares and the discharge of subsisting obligations; register of buy-back in Form SH-10 and return in Form SH-11 within 30 days of completion

Section 69: on a buy-back out of free reserves or the securities premium account, a sum equal to the nominal value of the shares purchased is transferred to the capital redemption reserve, disclosed in the balance sheet, and applicable only for fully paid bonus shares

Section 70: no buy-back through any subsidiary company or through any investment company or group of investment companies; none while a default subsists in repayment of deposits or interest, redemption of debentures or preference shares, payment of dividend, or repayment of a term loan or interest to a bank or financial institution — permitted again only after the default is remedied and three years have lapsed; and none unless ss. 92, 123, 127 and 129 have been complied with
